offence_severity: imprisonment for a term which may extend to imprisonment for life
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged under Sections 304-B and 498-A IPC, both upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found premeditation/planning as the husband doused the victim in kerosene and set her on fire
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the second part of the dying declaration, which inspired confidence, and the evidence of the father of the deceased and the dying declaration that proved the demand of dowry and harassment soon before the death.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, particularly the father of the deceased and the mother of the deceased, as they provided evidence of the demand of dowry and harassment, and the dying declaration was considered reliable despite its initial contradiction.
bail_history: Bail bond stands cancelled. Appellant is directed to be taken into custody forthwith to serve the remainder period of sentence.
trial_duration: Offence: 1st March, 1996; Trial judgment: 1st August, 1997; High Court decision: 3rd February, 2010; Supreme Court decision: 2nd July, 2014
legal_representation: K. K. Mohan for the Appellant; Anil Kaushik, Kamal Mohan Gupta for the Respondent
investigation_status: First Information Report recorded, case converted under Section 304-B IPC, investigation completed, challan presented, accused charged
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction under Sections 304-B and 498-A IPC; High Court: Affirmed conviction; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the victim-deceased was subjected to cruelty and harassment in connection with the demand of dowry. The deceased received burn injuries nine months after marriage and made a dying declaration implicating her husband in the incident. The prosecution contended that the husband had doused her in kerosene and set her on fire, leading to her death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the medical evidence contradicted the prosecution's narrative, as the deceased's burns were not on the back, which would have been expected if she was doused in kerosene from behind. They also claimed the dying declaration was contradictory and unreliable, with the first part being tutored by the husband.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle under Section 304-B of the Indian Penal Code and Section 113-B of the Evidence Act, which presumes that the accused caused the dowry death if the essential ingredients are proved, including the death occurring within seven years of marriage, not under normal circumstances, and due to cruelty or harassment in connection with dowry demands.
precedent_relied_upon: Hira Lal & Ors. Vs. State (Govt. of NCT), Delhi (2003) 8 SCC 80
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution successfully proved the dowry death, and the trial court and High Court correctly convicted the accused under Section 304-B IPC. The court also found the accused guilty under Section 498-A IPC for subjecting the deceased to harassment.
